title: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: trabeculae lie along the principal stress trajectories \sigma_1, \sigma_2, crossing at 90^\circ

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: and we have no difficulty in seeing that the anatomical arrangement of the trabeculae follows precisely the mechanical distribution of compressive and tensile stress or, in other words, accords perfectly with the theoretical stress-diagram of the crane.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVI, “On Form and Mechanical Efficiency”; topic “Trabecular architecture and stress lines”. Scope: cancellous bone of weight-bearing vertebrate bones (femur, tibia, calcaneus)

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: trabeculae lie along the principal stress trajectories \sigma_1, \sigma_2, crossing at 90^\circ

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch16-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern fabric analysis and finite elements map well to the statement. Open micro-CT can test selected bones and species, but paired loading information and broad coverage are limited, and several loading histories can yield similar fabric.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate trabecular fabric tensors from micro-CT and principal stress directions from finite-element models under physiological loads, then test alignment and orthogonal crossing. Random or consistently oblique architecture would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Stress estimates depend on uncertain boundary and muscle loads.

Resolution is inadequate in many whole-bone scans.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Trabecular orientation and a finite-element stress map are both computable with existing methods, and some open micro-CT already resolves individual trabeculae. The classic crane comparison needs an intact loaded bone, which is less often deposited than small plugs. Because the stress field depends on boundary conditions that are not in the same files, agreement is informative and still open to circular loading assumptions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From micro-CT, extract trabecular orientations in the femoral head and compare them with principal-stress trajectories from a finite-element model of the same bone under stance loads, including a test that the two families cross near 90 degrees. Alignment well above a randomized or isotropic fabric would support the claim; a weak correlation or non-orthogonal crossings would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Principal-stress directions change with the assumed joint loads, so a model can be tuned toward the anatomy.

Many open micro-CT volumes are excised cylinders rather than intact femoral heads under physiological boundary conditions.
